content: In 1955, Lendrum proposed that pulmonary edema resulting from congestive heart failure might play a role in the development of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). This hypothesis led researchers to explore the use of digitalis glycosides, such as digoxin, to enhance myocardial contractility and alleviate congestive heart failure in affected neonates. The first documented use of digitalis glycosides in infants with RDS was reported by Stahlman in 1959. In an uncontrolled trial, Stahlman observed a reduction in mortality among infants with RDS who were treated with digitalis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of digoxin on mortality in premature infants who were either at risk for or diagnosed with RDS. To achieve this, comprehensive searches were conducted across multiple databases, including the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, Medline, CINHAL, and Embase. The search strategy utilized MeSH terms such as digoxin and digitalis, with filters applied for age groups (newborns and infants) and publication types (clinical trials). Additional sources, such as previous reviews, cross-references, conference proceedings, and expert consultations, were also included. The search was last updated in December 2008. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated the use of digoxin for either the prevention or treatment of RDS. Data on clinical outcomes were extracted from the trial reports by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. The analysis adhered to the methodological standards established by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Two randomized controlled trials were identified that examined the effects of digoxin in the context of RDS prevention and treatment. The findings from these trials did not demonstrate any improvement in respiratory status or reduction in mortality associated with digoxin use. A meta-analysis of the data revealed no significant benefit of digoxin treatment for infants at risk of or diagnosed with RDS. Specifically, the typical relative risk for mortality was 1.27 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78 to 2.07), and the typical risk difference was 0.06 (95% CI: -0.06 to 0.17). The authors concluded that while hemodynamic disturbances are involved in the broader pathogenesis of RDS, early congestive heart failure (excluding cases related to hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus) does not appear to be a major contributing factor. Consequently, the use of digoxin has not been shown to provide any therapeutic benefit in infants with RDS.
